newsitem.title: UK: Precious Metals Outlook - Palladium woes continue.
newsitem.headline: Precious Metals Outlook - Palladium woes continue.

text.p: Three consecutive days of limit up trading on Tokyo's Tocom palladium futures last week markets summed up the dilemma in platinum group metals (PGMs) market.

The world's largest exporter of palladium and second biggest shipper of platinum has resumed exporting for the first time since last December yet despite sporadic deliveries to Japan and Europe, the price of the metals refuses to fall.
In Europe, platinum fixed at 442.00 on Monday, its highest level since early June when it hit a seven-year high of $495 per ounce.
Palladium fixed at $233.00, just $7 short of its 17-year peak recorded on June 6.

"There is still a great deal of sorting out to be done in this market. Just because the Russians have landed a couple of shipments in Japan and offered some small parcels in Europe doesn't change anything that much," one dealer said.
The Japanee investors were caught out not only by the refusal of the underlying dollar priced commodities to beccome cheaper but also by the strength in the dollar.
"Even if platinum and palladium prices had come down, they would still have had to cover or meet margin calls as the yen prices was being forced up," one market analyst said.
Several things have combined to force platinum and especially palladium prices higher. They are both suffering from a lack of material available to European dealers.
In Japan, after six months of living off stocks Japanese end-users are anxious to rebuild inventories.
Russian shipments so far have been sufficiently light to ensure that neither dealers or consumers demands will be satisfied quickly.
Both metals are used in electronics and in the catalytic converters which neutralise noxious gases in car exhaust fumes and in a string of chemical and industrial applications.
In addition, palladium is used in dental alloys and platinum is used in jewellery, especially in Japan.

World supply of the metals are measured in hundreds of tonnes and Russia supplies 60 percent of palladium where it is the leading supplier and about 25 percent of platinum supply in which it is second behind South Africa.
Some consumers and dealers are concerned that Russia does not have the material to meet demand.
But precious metals markets analyst Andy Smith of Union Bank of Switzerland said, "It is risible to suggest that they don't have the metal."

Another analyst noted that as Russia had been producing the metals -- they are produced as by products of nickel at Russia's huge Norilsk mining and refining combine in Siberia -- stocks must have been building all year.
Dealers said small parcels of palladium had begun to arrive in Europe after some dealers signed contracts with the Russian export agency Almazjuvelirexport but no platinum.
"They seem to be selling just enough to keep the market ticking over but not lower the price," one dealer said.
"Last year's price for platinum was far too low (it averaged $397.32 vs 424.22 in 1995) so the platinum price is about right now. But palladium is expensive at anything over $170," he added.

UBS's Smith noted a comparison with the beleaguered gold market where prices have barely recovered from 12-year lows plumbed after the Australian central bank announced in July that it had sold 167 tonnes of gold from its reserves.

"There is a changing perception of the central banks (as potential sellers of gold and destroyers of the price) in the gold market and for the PGMs, Russia's role of supplier (changing to market manipulator instead of benign exporter)," he said.
-- Brian Spoors London Newsroom +44 171 542 8058
